overview: Dromiceiomimus (meaning 'emu mimic') was a medium-sized ornithomimosaurian theropod from the Late Cretaceous of Alberta, Canada, living approximately 74–70 million years ago. Estimated at around 3.5 metres in length and about 100 kilograms, it superficially resembled a modern ostrich or emu, with long hindlimbs, a lightly built body, and a toothless beak. It is currently regarded as a nomen dubium by many researchers, meaning the material attributed to it is no longer considered to reliably diagnose a species distinct from other ornithomimids.

Dromiceiomimus brevitertius was named by Dale Russell in 1972 from the Horseshoe Canyon Formation of Alberta. Questions about its validity stem from difficulties in separating it from Ornithomimus based on available skeletal material. The taxon illustrates broader challenges in ornithomimid taxonomy, where multiple closely related species in the same formation can be difficult to distinguish without multiple well-preserved specimens.

articles.title: Discovery and Naming
articles.body: Dromiceiomimus brevitertius was described by Dale Russell in 1972 from skeletal material in the Horseshoe Canyon Formation of Alberta. The genus name references the emu (Dromaius) of Australia, emphasising the animal's bird-like proportions, while the species epithet brevitertius refers to the proportionally short third metatarsal.

articles.title: Nomen Dubium Status
articles.body: Many subsequent assessments have concluded that Dromiceiomimus cannot be reliably distinguished from Ornithomimus based on available diagnostic features. The NHM notes it is now widely treated as a nomen dubium. This does not mean the specimens are unimportant — they contribute to understanding ornithomimid anatomy — but the genus name itself is of uncertain validity.

articles.title: Locomotion and Speed
articles.body: Ornithomimids like Dromiceiomimus were almost certainly among the fastest non-avian dinosaurs, with long, slender hindlimbs and a lightly built frame conducive to high running speeds. Biomechanical estimates for comparable ornithomimids suggest top speeds potentially exceeding 50 km/h, though such figures carry significant uncertainty.

articles.title: Diet and Ecology
articles.body: Ornithomimids are generally inferred to have been omnivores, using their toothless beaks to consume a variety of plant material, insects, small vertebrates, and possibly eggs. The absence of teeth and the structure of the forelimbs suggest a generalist opportunistic diet rather than specialised predation.

record.description: Dromiceiomimus brevitertius is an ornithomimid name based on Canadian Late Cretaceous skull and skeletal material. It was long synonymized with Ornithomimus edmontonicus, but renewed anatomical work has argued that a distinct, slender-limbed taxon may be recognisable.
facts: The page must present the synonymy debate, not one resolution as settled fact.
Toothless jaws and long cursorial limbs are documented for the referred ornithomimid material.
Diet remains unresolved and should not be labelled confidently as herbivorous or carnivorous.
